clinicalPearls: H. influenzae is a small, pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus that often stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum, so it is easily overlooked on Gram stain.

Aerobic growth of H. influenzae requires both hemin (X factor) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (V factor) and needs preheated blood, so it grows on chocolate agar but not on ordinary (unheated) blood agar.

Six capsular serotypes (a-f) exist plus unencapsulated nontypeable strains; type b (Hib) and nontypeable strains are the most clinically important, with Hib being invasive (hematogenous spread) and nontypeable being primarily mucosal pathogens.

Maternally acquired anticapsular (anti-PRP) antibody declines from birth to about 6 months; the antibody nadir corresponds to the peak age of type b disease, and systemic Hib disease is unusual after age 6 owing to acquired protective antibody.

Hib meningitis primarily affects children under 2 years; subdural effusion is the most common complication and should be suspected when seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation follow 2-3 days of appropriate therapy.

Hib epiglottitis is a life-threatening cellulitis of the epiglottis and supraglottic tissues occurring in an older age group (2-7 years) than other Hib infections; in countries with childhood Hib vaccination it now occurs mainly in adults.
Nontypeable H. influenzae is the most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations and, in recent years, has caused community-acquired pneumonia more frequently than S. pneumoniae.

Nontypeable H. influenzae is one of the three most common causes of childhood otitis media (with S. pneumoniae and M. catarrhalis); clinical clues include recurrent episodes, treatment failure, concomitant conjunctivitis, and bilateral disease.

Invasive nontypeable strains causing neonatal/puerperal sepsis after colonizing the female genital tract have been provisionally named Haemophilus quentini (related to but distinct from H. haemolyticus).

Moraxella catarrhalis is an unencapsulated gram-negative diplococcus of the respiratory tract; its colonies can be slid intact across the agar surface (the hockey puck sign) and turn pink after 48 h, distinguishing them from commensal Neisseria.

M. catarrhalis is the second most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations after H. influenzae and accounts for roughly 15-20 percent of acute otitis media cases by middle-ear culture (30-50 percent by molecular detection).

Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer disease; prior chancroid does not confer protection, and H. ducreyi is also an important cause of non-sexually transmitted cutaneous ulcers in children in the South Pacific and Africa.
harrison.pathophysiology: Hib strains produce systemic disease by invading the respiratory mucosa and spreading hematogenously to distant sites such as meninges, bones, and joints; the type b polysaccharide capsule (ribosyl-ribitol phosphate) is a key virulence factor that resists opsonization. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule and cause disease by local mucosal invasion (e.g., otitis media via the eustachian tube, lower respiratory infection in COPD), persisting in airways both extracellularly and intracellularly and forming biofilms in the middle ear that resist host clearance and antibiotics; they vary expression of virulence genes by slipped-strand mispairing and phase-variable DNA methylases. M. catarrhalis colonizes the upper airway and infects by contiguous spread, often following a viral upper respiratory infection (e.g., rhinovirus promotes adhesion); it uses multiple adhesins, invades several cell types with an intracellular lymphoid reservoir, and sheds outer-membrane vesicles that deliver beta-lactamase and induce inflammation, potentially protecting co-pathogens such as group A streptococci and H. influenzae. H. ducreyi infects through an epithelial break during sexual contact, producing ulcers with predominantly T-cell infiltrate.
additionalDifferentials: Pneumococcal pneumonia and other bacterial pneumonias (clinically indistinguishable from H. influenzae pneumonia)
Bacterial meningitis due to other pathogens
Acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae or M. catarrhalis
For chancroid: primary syphilis, secondary syphilis (condyloma latum), genital herpes, donovanosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, and folliculitis
For H. ducreyi cutaneous ulcers: yaws (Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue)
infectionMimics: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis)
Moraxella catarrhalis vs commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture
Haemophilus haemolyticus, a respiratory commensal with identical growth requirements that can be mistaken for H. influenzae
Herpes simplex virus and Treponema pallidum in genital ulcer disease
additionalInvestigations: Culture from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, joint, pleural, pericardial fluid, or subdural effusion) is the most reliable means of diagnosing invasive H. influenzae and is needed for susceptibility testing
Gram stain of CSF showing gram-negative coccobacilli supports Hib meningitis; predominant gram-negative coccobacilli among abundant neutrophils in sputum suggests nontypeable H. influenzae pneumonia
PCR and other DNA-based detection methods, now common in clinical labs
Genotypic markers (16S rRNA, superoxide dismutase, outer-membrane protein P6, protein D, fuculose kinase) and whole-genome sequencing to distinguish H. influenzae from H. haemolyticus
Pneumatic otoscopy detects middle-ear fluid; tympanocentesis with culture gives etiologic diagnosis of otitis media but is not routine

For chancroid: culture of H. ducreyi (requires selective/supplemented media) from the lesion or node aspirate, and PCR; dark-field exam and syphilis serology to exclude T. pallidum and HSV testing of exudate
redFlags: Sore throat and fever rapidly progressing to dysphagia, drooling, and airway obstruction (epiglottitis) - a medical emergency requiring airway maintenance
Fever with altered CNS function and nuchal rigidity (which may be absent) in a young child suggesting Hib meningitis
Seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation after 2-3 days of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting subdural effusion
Underlying immunosuppression, HIV, cardiopulmonary disease, alcoholism, or cancer in a patient with H. influenzae bacteremia
harrison.prognosis: The overall mortality of Hib meningitis is about 5 percent with a high morbidity rate; about 6 percent of survivors have permanent sensorineural hearing loss, roughly one-fourth have a significant disability, and up to half have some neurologic sequela such as partial hearing loss or delayed language development when sought carefully. Hib epiglottitis is life-threatening due to risk of acute upper-airway obstruction. Glucocorticoids reduce the incidence of neurologic sequelae in Hib meningitis. Nontypeable strains tend to cause recurrent otitis media and recurrent COPD exacerbations because immunity is strain-specific. M. catarrhalis otitis media and exacerbations are clinically milder (less fever, less red bulging tympanic membrane) than pneumococcal disease, and invasive M. catarrhalis infection is rare. Repeated H. ducreyi infections can occur because infection confers no protection; in HIV-positive patients chancroid healing may be slow and require longer therapy.
pitfalls: H. influenzae may be missed on Gram stain because it stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum.
Ordinary (unheated) blood agar fails to grow H. influenzae, which can lead to false-negative cultures if chocolate agar is not used.
Distinguishing H. influenzae from the commensal H. haemolyticus is difficult because they share growth requirements and many H. haemolyticus isolates are now nonhemolytic.
M. catarrhalis has historically been overlooked as a pathogen because its colonies resemble those of commensal Neisseria species on respiratory cultures.

Approximately 30-40 percent of nontypeable H. influenzae produce beta-lactamase (conferring ampicillin/amoxicillin resistance), and a second mechanism, altered penicillin-binding proteins (beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant strains), is increasing in Europe and common in Japan.
Over 90 percent of M. catarrhalis strains now produce beta-lactamase and are resistant to amoxicillin; macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance is emerging, notably in Asia.
Clinical diagnosis of chancroid is often inaccurate, so laboratory confirmation should be attempted; in HIV-positive patients apparent treatment failure may reflect HSV co-infection.
Isolation of M. catarrhalis from expectorated sputum during an exacerbation is suggestive but not diagnostic of it as the cause.
